html:
In a world full of noise, have you ever wondered what would happen if every sound around you suddenly disappeared? At Microsoft’s headquarters in the United States there is a special room known as the quietest room in the world. Its noise level is as low as −20 dB SPL, and Guinness World Records has officially certified it as the lowest-noise environment on Earth.

But don’t picture it as the perfect place to meditate. Many people who step inside can clearly hear their own heartbeat, the blood flowing in their veins and their stomach at work, and some even feel dizzy, tense or panicky. Few people can stay inside for more than 30 minutes!

Image: Microsoft

Just how quiet is it?

Typical everyday noise levels are roughly:

  • An ordinary office: 40–50 dB SPL

  • A quiet library: 30 dB SPL

  • The threshold of human hearing (the theoretical minimum sound pressure): 0 dB SPL

The background noise in Microsoft’s room is just −20 dB SPL, meaning its sound pressure is below the quietest sound humans can perceive. This is an “ultra-quiet” level that only professional measuring instruments can detect.

How does it get so quiet?

The room is an anechoic chamber, literally a room “without echoes.” Its design minimizes both the transmission and the reflection of sound:

  • All six surfaces are lined with sound-absorbing wedges, a special material that absorbs more than 99% of the incident sound, so there is almost no echo.

  • The room itself “floats”: it is completely isolated from the building structure and rests on vibration isolators, which keep out structure-borne noise from the building.

  • Airflow, mechanical vibration and the like are all shut out, and the whole space is as silent as deep space.

Sound has nowhere to go, and your ears are left on a desert island.

What happens to people inside?

Once you are inside and all outside sound is blocked, the only sounds left are those coming from inside your own body:

  • your heartbeat;

  • blood rushing past your ears;

  • your bones and joints clicking;

  • your stomach and intestines gurgling;

  • even the changes in pressure as your eyeballs move.

Some visitors describe the experience as “unbearable”: “You find that the sound hasn’t disappeared. It’s all coming from you.”

Because the human brain relies on background noise to sense space and balance, total silence can upset your sense of direction and your sense of time, and may even trigger mild hallucinations. According to Microsoft engineers, very few people have managed to stay in the room for more than 45 minutes.

What is the room really for?

It may sound like a torture device, but it is in fact an engineering-grade test environment, used to:

  • test the background noise of devices (fans, electric motors, computer audio);

  • measure how quiet electronic products are (headphones, microphones, loudspeakers);

  • calibrate speech recognition systems, hearing aids, hearing screeners and other medical devices;

  • study how people react psychologically to extreme silence, and where their limits lie.

It has helped Microsoft improve the audio design of its own speakers, Surface tablets, Xbox consoles and other products.

Other ultra-quiet spaces

Besides Microsoft, a number of universities and research institutions have built similar anechoic chambers:

  • an anechoic chamber at the University of Minnesota once held the world record;

  • the UK’s National Physical Laboratory has similar facilities for aeroacoustics research;

  • several Chinese universities and laboratories have built national-level anechoic chambers.

Silence is not emptiness but presence at its most intense

The “quietest room in the world” shows us that when every outside sound is removed, you come face to face with the universe of sound inside your own body. It is a space as overwhelming as it is awe-inspiring. It challenges our idea of what “quiet” means and invites us to rethink the role of sound in our lives and in technology.
